subject: Polycarp of Smyrna

feasts.text: Catholic (General Roman Calendar): 23 February, an obligatory memorial, "Memorial of Saint Polycarp, Bishop and Martyr".
feasts.source: USCCB Daily Readings for 23 February 2022 (page title "Memorial of Saint Polycarp, Bishop and Martyr"); Calendarium Romanum 1969, list "Memoriae obligatoriae" (it counts sixty-three): "Februarius ... 23 S. Polycarpi."
feasts.note: Vatican News keeps him on 23 February too.

feasts.text: In Lent the memorial gives way. 23 February fell in Lent in 2026, and the USCCB calendar printed him in brackets on a "Lenten Weekday": "[Saint Polycarp, Bishop and Martyr]". The same calendar says brackets mark an optional memorial.
feasts.source: USCCB, Liturgical Calendar for the Dioceses of the United States of America, 2026: "23 Mon Lenten Weekday / [Saint Polycarp, Bishop and Martyr]"; "In this calendar, Optional Memorials are designated by the use of italics within brackets."
feasts.note: Detail for the writer, not needed on the page. 23 February falls in Lent again in 2027 (Ash Wednesday 10 February).

feasts.text: Catholic, before 1969: 26 January. The 1916 Roman Martyrology gives his "birthday" on 26 January, and the 1960 Roman calendar kept him on 26 January.
feasts.source: The Roman Martyrology (1916), 26 January: "At Smyrna, the birthday of St. Polycarp, a disciple of the Apostle St. John ..."; Calendarium Romanum 1969, commentary: "In calendario anni 1960 multi martyres non romani scripti erant: ... S. Polycarpus (26 ian.)".
feasts.note: Rank in the 1960/1962 calendar not checked (see could_not_verify).

feasts.text: Why Rome moved him in 1969: he died on 23 February, but his feast had been set on 26 January, the day another Polycarp, of Nicaea, died. The 1969 calendar gives him as its example of saints "confused with others".
feasts.source: Calendarium Romanum 1969, commentary, "Recognitio diei festi Sanctorum": "Multi dies falsi sunt; nonnulli Sancti cum aliis confusi sunt; v. g., S. Polycarpus martyrium subiit die 23 februarii (anno circiter 156), sed eius festum die 26 ianuarii statutum est, quo die S. Polycarpus Nicaenus obiit." Footnote 17: "Cf. Breviarium Syriacum, ed. B. Mariani, Roma 1956, p. 30."
feasts.note: The same passage opens with the Smyrnaeans' own words on keeping the anniversary (Martyrdom, chapter 18), as the reason saints are kept on the day they died. Plain rendering for the page: "Rome kept him on 26 January until 1969. That was the day another Polycarp, of Nicaea, died. The new calendar put him back on the day he died." The 1969 text says "about 156".

feasts.text: In the 1916 Roman Martyrology, 23 February belongs to a different Polycarp: "At Rome, St. Polycarp, priest, who with blessed Sebastian converted many to the faith of Christ". The bishop of Smyrna is on 26 January.
feasts.source: The Roman Martyrology (1916), 23 February; index: "Polycarp, St., B., M., and 12 others Jan. 26 / Polycarp, St., Pr., M. Feb. 23 / Polycarp, St., M. Dec. 7".
feasts.note: A possible "Did you know?" tidbit: for centuries his own death-day in the Roman book belonged to a Roman priest of the same name. The 1916 entry also says twelve others "from Philadelphia" suffered with him (the Martyrdom, chapter 19, counts him the twelfth, with those from Philadelphia).

feasts.text: Orthodox Church in America: 23 February, "Hieromartyr Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna".
feasts.source: OCA, Lives of the Saints: "Hieromartyr Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna / Commemorated on February 23".
feasts.note: The OCA's life follows the later legend (the widow Kallista, Bucolus, an angel): do not use it for facts.

feasts.text: Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America: 23 February, "Polycarp the Holy Martyr & Bishop of Smyrna". Its hymns call him "Hieromartyr Polycarp".
feasts.source: GOARCH, Chapel, Saints, contentid 439: title and "February 23"; "Apolytikion of Hieromartyr Polycarp".
feasts.note: The live page answers 403 to scripts; the text was read from the Wayback copy of 21 February 2024 (https://web.archive.org/web/20240221210816/https://www.goarch.org/chapel/saints?contentid=439). GOARCH dates his death "about the year 163".

feasts.text: Greek synaxaria: 23 February. saint.gr: "Εορτάζει στις 23 Φεβρουαρίου εκάστου έτους" (kept on 23 February every year). synaxarion.gr lists him on 23 February as "Ὁ Ἅγιος Πολύκαρπος ὁ Ἱερομάρτυρας Ἐπίσκοπος Σμύρνης".
feasts.source: saint.gr, "Άγιος Πολύκαρπος Επίσκοπος Σμύρνης"; synaxarion.gr, day list for 23 February (https://www.synaxarion.gr/gr/m/2/d/23/sxsaintlist.aspx).
feasts.note: saint.gr gives the arrest in 167 and a legendary birth (about 80, to Pancratius and Theodora).

feasts.text: Russian Orthodox Church (old calendar): 23 February, which is 8 March on today's civil calendar. Azbuka Very prints "День памяти 8 марта" and calls him священномученик (hieromartyr).
feasts.source: azbyka.ru, "Поликарп Смирнский": "День памяти / 8 марта"; "Житие священномученика Поликарпа, епископа Смирнского".

feasts.text: Coptic Orthodox Church: 29 Amshir, "The Martyrdom of St. Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna". 29 Amshir falls on 8 March in the civil calendar.
feasts.source: CopticChurch.net, Synaxarium, Amshir 29 (sponsored by St. Mark's Coptic Orthodox Church, Jersey City).
feasts.note: The page does not print the civil date. The conversion is ours: copticchurch.net showed 25 September 2026 as 15 Tout, so 1 Tout is 11 September, and 29 Amshir (day 179) is 8 March 2027. So the Coptic and Russian days fall on the same civil day. The Coptic synaxarium's story differs from the Martyrdom: it dates his death to 167 and says the governor "ordered to cut off his head". Use it for the date only.

feasts.text: Church of England (Common Worship): 23 February, "Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna, Martyr, c.155". A Lesser Festival: it is printed in roman type, and the calendar prints Commemorations in italics.
feasts.source: Church of England, Common Worship, The Calendar. The page says "Commemorations are printed in italics"; the HTML has no <em> round the Polycarp line (Valentine on 14 February, a Commemoration, has one).

feasts.text: Episcopal Church (Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022): 23 February, "Polycarp of Smyrna, Bishop and Martyr, 156".
feasts.source: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, pages 107-108: the Polycarp entry runs under the page header "February 23", with collects and lessons (Revelation 2:8-11, Psalm 121, Matthew 20:20-28).
feasts.note: In the text extraction the calendar table's day numbers print one line above their names (Polycarp shows as 22, Matthias as 23): trust the page header. LFF's own prose: "It probably occurred in the year 156."

feasts.text: Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod (Lutheran Service Book): 23 February, "Polycarp of Smyrna, Pastor and Martyr".
feasts.source: LCMS, Commemorations: "23 - Polycarp of Smyrna, Pastor and Martyr"; CPH, Complete List of Church Year Commemorations (the same).
feasts.note: The LSB biography: "Born c. 69 ... executed for his faith on February 23, c. 156."

feasts.text: ELCA (Evangelical Lutheran Worship): 23 February, "Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna, martyr, 156". A commemoration: it is printed in lower case, and the lesser festivals are in capitals. Colour scarlet or red.
feasts.source: Evangelical Lutheran Worship, The Church Year, assembly version, final draft January 2006; confirmed current by the Grand Canyon Synod of the ELCA, February 2024: "Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna, martyr, died 156 (Feb 23)".
feasts.note: The ELW text is the 2006 final draft (the printed book was not checked); the 2024 synod list (https://www.gcsynod.org/news/for-what-shall-we-pray-2024-02-02) confirms the date.

feast_table.rank: Memorial (obligatory); in Lent printed as optional
Holy Martyr and Bishop (Hieromartyr in the hymns)
Lesser feast with its own collects

why_the_dates.text: Why 23 February: the Martyrdom dates his death to "the seventh before the calends of March, on a great Sabbath, at the eighth hour", the second day of Xanthicus, when Statius Quadratus was proconsul. The seventh day before the kalends of March is 23 February.
why_the_dates.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 21: Lightfoot 1891 ("on the seventh before the calends of March"); Kirsopp Lake 1912 ("the seventh day before the kalends of March").
why_the_dates.note: WARNING: the Roberts-Donaldson text in ANF 1 reads "the seventh day before the Kalends of May", and its note admits "Great obscurity hangs over the chronology here". Quote chapter 21 from Lightfoot or Lake, not ANF. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1911) reads "March" too.

why_the_dates.text: The Smyrnaeans themselves meant to keep the day. The Martyrdom says they laid his bones in a fit place, where they would gather each year for "the birthday of his martyrdom".
why_the_dates.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 18; the Calendarium Romanum 1969 quotes this passage in Latin as the root of keeping saints on the day they died.
why_the_dates.note: Take the exact English from Lightfoot or ANF (the quotation researchers). ANF's note: "Literally, 'the birth-day.'"

why_the_dates.text: The churches agree on the day but not the year. Church of England "c.155"; Vatican News "February 23rd in the year 155"; the Episcopal Church and the ELCA 156, the LCMS "c. 156"; the 1969 Roman calendar "about 156"; GOARCH "about the year 163"; saint.gr and the Coptic synaxarium 167.
why_the_dates.source: Each church page as listed under feasts; Vatican News; Calendarium Romanum 1969.
why_the_dates.note: The scholars' case, from the Catholic Encyclopedia (1911): W. H. Waddington, followed by Lightfoot, put Statius Quadratus's proconsulship in 154-155, so 23 February 155; Schmid argued for 166; Eusebius and Jerome put the death under Marcus Aurelius. The Encyclopedia adds that "the subscription" may have been "tampered with by a later hand". Our own calendar check: 23 February was a Saturday in 155 and in 166, a Sunday in 156 (the Martyrdom says "a great Sabbath"). That check is ours; do not print it without a source.

is_he_a_saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans count him a saint, and Lutherans remember him too.

churches.note: A Lesser Festival in the Church of England

items.text: Catholic: a saint and martyr, with an obligatory memorial in the General Roman Calendar.
items.source: USCCB; Calendarium Romanum 1969; Vatican News, "St. Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna and Martyr".

items.text: Orthodox: a saint and hieromartyr (a martyr who was a bishop or priest) in the OCA, the Greek Archdiocese, the Greek synaxaria and the Russian Church.
Oriental Orthodox: the Coptic synaxarium keeps "The Martyrdom of St. Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna" on 29 Amshir.
items.note: Armenian: not verified (see could_not_verify). The page may add "and the Coptic Church" to the big line if it wants.

items.text: Anglican: a Lesser Festival in the Church of England; kept with its own collects in the Episcopal Church.
items.source: Common Worship calendar; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022.

items.text: Lutheran: commemorated by the LCMS ("Pastor and Martyr") and the ELCA ("Bishop of Smyrna, martyr").
items.source: LCMS Commemorations; ELW; Grand Canyon Synod 2024.

items.text: He was honoured from the first. The church of Smyrna gathered his bones and meant to keep the day of his death each year.
items.note: No fetched source says he was "the first" saint or martyr to have a yearly feast. Say what chapter 18 says, never "first".

also_called.source: OCA title "Hieromartyr Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna"; GOARCH hymns "Hieromartyr Polycarp"; synaxarion.gr "ὁ Ἱερομάρτυρας"; azbyka.ru "священномученик".
Merriam-Webster: "Saint 2nd century Christian martyr and Apostolic Father; bishop of Smyrna"; Britannica: "a Greek bishop of Smyrna and an Apostolic Father".

also_called.text: "An apostolic and prophetic teacher" and bishop of the church in Smyrna, in the Martyrdom itself.
also_called.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 16. ANF: "having in our own times been an apostolic and prophetic teacher, and bishop of the Catholic Church which is in Smyrna". Lightfoot: "an apostolic and prophetic teacher in our own time, a bishop of the holy Church which is in Smyrna".
also_called.note: The two translations differ ("Catholic" against "holy"): quote one exactly.

also_called.text: "The teacher of Asia, the father of the Christians": the crowd's cry in the stadium.
also_called.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp, chapter 12 (ANF and Lightfoot both).

also_called.text: "That blessed and apostolic presbyter": Irenaeus's words for him.
also_called.source: Irenaeus, Letter to Florinus, in Eusebius, Church History, Book 5, chapter 20 (McGiffert).

also_called.text: Church titles in the West: "Saint Polycarp, Bishop and Martyr" (Catholic); "Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna, Martyr" (Church of England); "Polycarp of Smyrna, Bishop and Martyr" (Episcopal); "Polycarp of Smyrna, Pastor and Martyr" (LCMS).

in_art.text: In Western art: stabbed and burnt, with a pile of burning wood near him, or burnt at a stake.
in_art.source: F. C. Husenbeth, Emblems of Saints (third edition, 1882): "S. Polycarp, B. M. (26 Jan.) 166 / Stabbed, and burnt to death / Pile of wood in flames near him / Burnt at a stake".
in_art.note: Husenbeth still uses the old 26 January and the year 166.

in_art.text: In Orthodox icons: an old man with a rounded beard, among the holy bishops.
in_art.source: The Byzantine painter's guide of Dionysius of Fourna, in Didron's French edition (1845), section "Les saints évêques": "Saint Polycarpe de Smyrne : vieillard, barbe arrondie."
in_art.note: Plain page wording: "An old bishop with a rounded beard. In the West, a bishop at the stake, with flames or a pile of wood."

in_art.text: No ancient church in England was dedicated to him (nor to Ignatius).
in_art.source: Francis Bond, Dedications and Patron Saints of English Churches (1914): "Yet we have no ancient church dedicated either to Ignatius or to Polycarp."
in_art.note: Minor; a tidbit only if the writer wants it.

pronounced.note: Merriam-Webster's first vowel (ä) is the o of American "cot", so "POL-ee-karp" suits American and British readers alike. Collins answered 403 and was not read.

wrote.text: One work survives: his Letter to the Philippians.
wrote.source: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, chapter 3, part 4: "There is also a very powerful Epistle of Polycarp written to the Philippians"; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 17: "He wrote a very valuable Epistle to the Philippians which is read to the present day in the meetings in Asia."

wrote.text: Other letters are lost. Irenaeus says they could still be read in his day: "the letters which he sent, either to the neighboring churches for their confirmation, or to some of the brethren, admonishing and exhorting them".
wrote.source: Irenaeus, Letter to Florinus, in Eusebius, Church History, Book 5, chapter 20 (McGiffert).

wrote.text: Plain page wording for "Wrote": "One letter, to the church at Philippi. Irenaeus knew others, now lost."

reference.text: Wikipedia: "Polycarp". Wikidata: Q192371 (label "Polycarp", description "bishop of Smyrna and martyr (69–155)").
reference.source: Wikipedia REST summary (title "Polycarp", wikibase_item Q192371); Wikidata Special:EntityData/Q192371.json; design/saints-hub/research/wikidata-qids.json agrees.
reference.note: sameAs: ["https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polycarp", "https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q192371"]. Wikidata stores his death as 23 February 155 in the Julian calendar; the local wd-*.json files show 22 February because their query converted it. Wikidata gives Smyrna as his birthplace with no source.

reference.text: deathPlace: Smyrna, in the Roman province of Asia; today Izmir in Turkey.
reference.source: Martyrdom of Polycarp (Smyrna, throughout); Merriam-Webster, Izmir: "or formerly Smyrna ... city and port on the Gulf of Izmir ... in western Turkey".

reference.text: birthPlace: unknown. No early source says where he was born.
reference.source: The Martyrdom, Irenaeus, Eusebius and Jerome are silent. Wikidata says Smyrna without a source. The later Life ascribed to Pionius says he was bought as a boy from the East; saint.gr gives him parents named Pancratius and Theodora.
reference.note: Leave person.birthPlace out (the type allows it).

reference.text: Born about 69 or 70. The churches reckon it from his "eighty-six years" (Martyrdom, chapter 9) and a death in 155 or 156.
reference.source: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022: "Polycarp, born in the year 69"; LSB: "Born c. 69"; Vatican News: "Born between 69 and 70AD".
reference.note: Band dates: "About 69 to 155". The text only says he had served Christ eighty-six years; that may count from his baptism, not his birth.

reference.text: alternateName for JSON-LD: "Saint Polycarp", "Polycarp of Smyrna", "Hieromartyr Polycarp", "Polycarpus".
reference.source: OCA; Wikidata aliases ("Polycarp of Smyrna", "Bishop Polycarp"); Latin "S. Polycarpus" in the Calendarium Romanum.

hub_filters.note: types.ts lists an "apostolic" group key, but GROUPS in site/src/lib/saints/data.ts has no "apostolic" option, so the hub has no such filter today. Add "apostolic" only if that group goes live; he is its model.

hub_filters.source: He lived, taught and died at Smyrna in Asia (Martyrdom; Irenaeus). He went to Rome once, under Anicetus, and went home (Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 3, chapter 3; his letter to Victor in Eusebius, Church History, Book 5, chapter 24).
hub_filters.note: Irenaeus's page uses "east west" because he moved to Gaul; Polycarp only visited Rome. The 1916 Martyrology says he sent missionaries to Gaul (Benignus, Andochius, Andeol): later legend, not grounds for "west".

hub_filters.text: alias: "polycarpus polykarp polykarpos policarpo polycarpe smyrna izmir hieromartyr apostolic father".
hub_filters.source: Latin, German, Greek, Italian/Spanish and French forms; the place names people search with.
hub_filters.note: The hub search already finds "polycarp", so "saint polycarp" adds nothing.

facts_rows.Also called: **Hieromartyr Polycarp**, in the Orthodox churches. An **Apostolic Father**.
facts_rows.Status: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans. Lutherans remember him too.
facts_rows.In art: An old bishop with a rounded beard. In the West, a bishop at the stake, with flames or a pile of wood.
facts_rows.Wrote: One letter, to the church at Philippi. Irenaeus knew others, now lost.

west.text: His day in the **1916 Roman Martyrology**, and in the Roman calendar until 1969.
**Catholic** memorial. Also the **Church of England**, the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.

east.text: The **OCA**, the **Greek** churches, and the **Russian Church** on the old calendar.
The **Coptic** Church, on 29 Amshir in its own calendar.

feasts.note: Why 23 February? The letter about his death gives the day: the seventh before the kalends of March. Rome kept him on 26 January until 1969. That was the day another Polycarp, of Nicaea, died. The new calendar put him back. Churches on the old calendar keep 23 February 13 days later, on 8 March.

saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans count him a saint, and Lutherans remember him too.

churches.note: A Lesser Festival in the Church of England

leads_for_other_researchers: Heinrich Ignaz Franz Biber's "Sonata Sancti Polycarpi" for eight trumpets: the OCA life mentions it (spelling the composer "Bibier"). Other researchers saved editions-bim-biber-polycarpi.txt and mcnaughtan-biber-polycarpi.txt. A strong "Did you know?" if their source holds.
The Martyrdom, chapter 21, in ANF reads "Kalends of May": quote the date from Lightfoot or Lake.
The Coptic synaxarium says he was beheaded; the Martyrdom says a dagger, after the fire failed. Not for the page unless the writer wants to show how later retellings drifted.
The 1916 Martyrology's stories that Polycarp sent Benignus (Dijon), Andochius, Thyrsus and Felix (Autun) and Andeol (Vivarais) to Gaul: later tradition; mark as such if used.

could_not_verify.text: Patron saint of earache, hearing problems and dysentery.
could_not_verify.source: Britannica's question-and-answer box: "St. Polycarp is the patron saint of people suffering from earache, hearing issues, and dysentery." Catholic Online: "Patron: against earache, dysentery". No church, diocese or dictionary of saints found. Britannica's article body does not say it.
could_not_verify.note: Leave "Patron of" off the page. At most "*Britannica* says he is invoked against earache", if the owner wants a line; Martin's "*Britannica* adds" line came from Britannica's article, not its question box.

could_not_verify.text: Armenian Apostolic Church: keeps him on a movable day (per Wikipedia and Fandom only).
could_not_verify.source: The Armenian Prelacy pages answered 403 or did not name him.
could_not_verify.note: Leave the Armenian Church off the page.

could_not_verify.text: Rank of his 26 January day in the 1960/1962 Roman calendar (a third-class feast is expected).
could_not_verify.source: Not checked in a 1962 Missal or the 1960 rubrics.
could_not_verify.note: The page needs only the date, which is verified.

could_not_verify.source: Read through the Wayback copy of 21 February 2024.
could_not_verify.note: Date and title are verified from that copy; fine for the page.

could_not_verify.text: That he was the first saint, or the first martyr, to have a yearly feast.
could_not_verify.source: No fetched source says so. The Martyrdom (chapter 18) records the plan to keep the day; the 1969 Calendarium quotes it as the root of the custom.

could_not_verify.text: The printed Evangelical Lutheran Worship (2006) book, as against its final draft.
could_not_verify.source: The draft and a 2024 ELCA synod list agree on 23 February.

could_not_verify.text: The Anglican Church of Canada, other Oriental churches and the Eastern Catholic calendars.
